doc.title: Helen Oakley Dance interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

title: Producing the Variety small-band records for Irving Mills
summary: She proposed Ellington small-band sessions with Cootie, Johnny, Barney, Rex; no rehearsal and no rivalry, just the Ellington family.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Exactly. The fact that Duke said it, that was enough you know. And so Irving Mills — I was brought into Mills’ office and that was the other half of my career, because as Stanley I think told you, Mills started these two record companies, Master Records was the top label, and Variety was the second. And I was the producer. I used to sit at this long table with about twenty accountants and people, and then they said to me, what have

you to say? And I said, and so somebody said, “She did those Goodman things, and she did this and she did that you see. And so I said, “We ought to make the small band records.” And I knew Duke would agree you see, because Duke, amongst other things, he had a very good head for what could make a bit of money. Because he needed to. How was he going to keep going if he didn’t? And so of course that was a very good idea, because for two years, well it went on after I left them, we just made the small bands. You know the small bands, don’t you? Well you know, so it was Cootie and Johnny that I wanted of course. And so Duke started off with Barney [Bigard] and with Lawrence [Brown] I think, and — yes Stanley’s saying something. Ray Nance? Rex, of course, who never really was able to show who he really was or how. You know he had a bit of a complex. I think his writing later shows you really who he is. But anyway, he was a wonderful musician. I mean with Fletcher Henderson, people knew that. He didn’t show up, to my mind, for what he really was. Duke established a personality for him and made him stay in it you know. Man with a horn, boy with a horn, and those things. But anyway that was great, great fun for a couple of years we made those small— No, we never rehearsed, we never did anything.
Was there competition among Duke’s men to want to be a part of these records?

No. I mean Duke’s men, you know, is another story as I know you must know. It was a complicated family, with all the family stories that are in families. There were ins and outs and they changed sometimes and so on. No, nobody ever, you never saw the face of people you know. As you know, Johnny Hodges had a complete, immovable face, no matter what gorgeous thing he was playing. And so they had little things. I mean Johnny and Barney had, they sat next to one another. They had a little something at times. But mostly everything, it was the Ellington band, and as a family, nobody else knew. It was family affairs. And they quietly carried on their family affairs. It was very, very interesting.
